meta.title: Who really said "The object in life is not to be on the side of the majority, but to escape finding oneself in the ranks of the insane"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not from the Meditations. The line is a paraphrase from the close of Tolstoy's 1904 essay 'Bethink Yourselves!', a block Tolstoy himself signed 'Marcus Aurelius.'
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The object in life is not to be on the side of the majority, but to escape finding oneself in the ranks of the insane'?
meta.ogDescription: It isn't in Marcus Aurelius's Meditations. It's a paraphrase from Tolstoy's 1904 essay 'Bethink Yourselves!' — signed, by Tolstoy, 'Marcus Aurelius.'

answer.label: Not from Marcus Aurelius — a Tolstoy paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: Nothing resembling this line appears in Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations. Its earliest documented home is the anthology of maxims that closes Leo Tolstoy’s 1904 anti-war essay ‘Bethink Yourselves!’, where Tolstoy strings together Stoic-flavoured lines and signs the block ‘Marcus Aurelius’ — a free paraphrase, not a quotation from any surviving text. Wikiquote files it under ‘Misattributed.’

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: trans. Aylmer Maude, in ‘Recollections and Essays’ (Oxford Univ. Press, 1946), p. 237

source.excerpt: … desire general welfare, and not personal as do the majority of men. The object of life is not to be on the side of the majority, but to escape finding oneself in the ranks of the insane. …
trail: The exact wording closes an anthology of maxims near the end of Tolstoy’s 1904 essay ‘Bethink Yourselves!’, printed as ‘The object of life is not to be on the side of the majority…’ and signed ‘Marcus Aurelius’ — right before a Kant passage.
Wikiquote lists it under ‘Misattributed’, tracing the first citation to the 1946 Oxford translation and noting nothing resembling it appears in the Meditations.
It is absent from the 1904 Project Gutenberg translation of the same essay — the exact English wording is translation-specific.
Quote sites and even Goodreads still file it under Marcus Aurelius, almost always with no source page named.
source.excerptNote: In Tolstoy’s essay this sits inside a compiled block of Stoic-sounding maxims that ends with the signature “MARCUS AURELIUS.” — and is immediately followed by a passage from Kant (“Sapere aude!”). It is Tolstoy’s loose paraphrase, not a line traceable to any surviving work of the emperor. Note the source prints “object of life”; the popular meme drifts to “object in life.”
source.rightsNote: The ancient Meditations is long in the public domain — but this line is not from it. The wording is a modern English translation-paraphrase drawn from Tolstoy’s essay; the earliest citation Wikiquote finds is a 1946 Oxford edition, so its exact-form provenance cannot be tied to a specific pre-1931 publication. Status is therefore left uncertain rather than claimed public-domain.

author.name: Leo Tolstoy
author.heading: How a Tolstoy paraphrase became ‘Marcus Aurelius’
author.bio: Tolstoy, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina, spent his later years as a radical Christian moralist and pacifist. His 1904 essay ‘Bethink Yourselves!’, written against the Russo-Japanese War, closes with a garland of borrowed maxims — one block of which Tolstoy attributes to Marcus Aurelius. It is inside that loosely rendered block that “the object of life… escape finding oneself in the ranks of the insane” first appears in English — a paraphrase that later circulated worldwide as a genuine Marcus Aurelius quotation.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet-name” misattribution: a stirring line pinned on Marcus Aurelius because it sounds Stoic, even though it never appears in his one surviving book.

items.why: No passage resembling “the side of the majority… the ranks of the insane” exists in the Meditations; Wikiquote classes it ‘Misattributed’. The wording is Tolstoy’s free paraphrase, which Tolstoy himself labelled ‘Marcus Aurelius.’
Quote databases that do name a book point to the Meditations, but the line is not there in any translation — the citation is invented after the fact to match the famous name.

misattribution.truthLine: The line’s earliest documented appearance is the closing anthology of Tolstoy’s ‘Bethink Yourselves!’ (1904) — a paraphrase that Tolstoy, not Marcus Aurelius, put into these words.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Marcus Aurelius is one of the internet’s biggest fake-quote magnets: a Roman emperor-philosopher whose real book, the Meditations, is a grab-bag of short aphorisms, so almost any Stoic-flavoured line can be slipped under his name and look plausible.

This one is unusual in that we can point to exactly where the English wording came from. Tolstoy, assembling wise sayings to close an anti-war essay, rendered a Marcus-Aurelius-themed block in his own paraphrase and signed it with the emperor’s name. Later readers lifted the punchy sentence out of Tolstoy’s prose and re-labelled it a direct quotation — the paraphrase became ‘the quote.’
context.detailsSummary: The fuller passage as Tolstoy printed it
detailsBody: In the 1946 Oxford text the block runs: “No one can coerce thy will… desire general welfare, and not personal as do the majority of men. The object of life is not to be on the side of the majority, but to escape finding oneself in the ranks of the insane…” and ends, several sentences later, “…has endowed them with freedom to become reconciled to each other after dissension. MARCUS AURELIUS.”

The very next quotation Tolstoy prints — “Enlightenment is the escape of man from his own childishness… Sapere aude!” — is Kant, underlining that these are Tolstoy’s hand-picked, freely rendered epigraphs rather than verbatim citations.
context.pull: The words are Tolstoy’s paraphrase; the byline he gave them is Marcus Aurelius’s.
